lead: A signal flow graph draws the same equations as a block diagram using only nodes and directed branches. A node is a signal; a branch is a gain. Mason's gain formula then gives the transfer function by counting forward paths and loops, with no step-by-step redrawing. It exists because block diagram reduction gets slow when several loops share blocks. Engineers use it on multi-loop hardware — motor speed loops, feedback amplifiers, process control loops — and examiners use it to check whether you can count loops correctly.
prereq: You need: transfer functions (1.3) and block diagram reduction (1.8).

sections.h3: Signals become nodes, blocks become branches

blocks.text: A signal flow graph (SFG) is a directed graph that carries exactly the same information as the equations of the system. Each node is one signal, written by its name: R, E, C. Each branch is a directed line from one node to another, and its branch gain (also called transmittance) is written beside it. The relation y = a·x is drawn as a branch from node x to node y with gain a.

A node with only outgoing branches is a source node; it holds the input R(s). A node with only incoming branches is a sink node; it holds the output C(s). Every other node has both, and that is where signals get added.

items: Take every signal in the block diagram — input, error, output of each block, output of each summing point — as one node.
Take every block of transfer function G as a branch of gain G from its input node to its output node.
Take every summing point as a node; each input to it enters as a branch of gain +1, −1 or the feedback gain.
A signal used at two places is one node with two outgoing branches, so take-off points need no extra nodes.
A negative feedback path from C to the summing point becomes a branch from C to the error node with gain −H.

blocks.text: A forward path goes from the source to the sink without visiting any node twice. Its path gain Pk is the product of the branch gains on it. A loop is a closed path that starts and ends at the same node without visiting any other node twice. Its loop gain Li is the product of branch gains around it, sign included: a branch of gain −H makes the loop gain negative.
Two loops are non-touching when they share no node at all. Sharing even one node makes them touching, and touching loops never appear together in one product.

blocks.where: Li is the gain of the i-th loop; LiLj is the product of one pair of non-touching loops; LiLjLk is a product of three mutually non-touching loops; signs alternate. Δ is the graph determinant.
Pk is the gain of the k-th forward path; Δk is Δ recomputed after deleting every loop that touches path k; if a path touches all loops, Δk = 1.

blocks.text: Δk is not a fresh formula. Write Δ, cross out the terms of the loops that touch path k, and what remains is Δk. A path that touches no loop keeps Δk = Δ.

sections.h3: Working order, and counting loops safely

items: List the nodes in signal order, source first.
Find every forward path from source to sink and write each Pk as a product.
Find every loop and write each Li with its sign; count a set of nodes once, whichever way round you walk it.
Compare node sets to separate touching loops from non-touching pairs and triples.
Build Δ term by term, then Δk for each path.
Substitute in T = ΣPkΔk / Δ and simplify.

blocks.text: A loop gain is negative when the loop holds an odd number of negative branches. With negative feedback, −ΣLi is positive, so Δ is larger than 1 — the same '1 + open-loop gain' that appears in the feedback rule of 1.8.
Two loops often look separate on paper but meet at one node. Test touching by listing nodes, never by looking at the drawing.

figure.caption: The forward path R→E→X→C carries gain G1G2. The single loop closes from C back to E with gain −H, so the loop gain is −G1G2H.

spec.aria: A signal flow graph with forward path R to E to X to C and one feedback loop from C to E with gain minus H.

examples.question: A negative-feedback system has forward blocks G1 = 2/(s+1) and G2 = 3/(s+2) in series, and feedback H = 1. Draw the signal flow graph and use Mason's gain formula to find C(s)/R(s).
steps: Nodes: R (source), E (error), X (output of G1), C (sink).
Branches: R→E gain 1; E→X gain G1; X→C gain G2; C→E gain −H = −1.
Forward paths: only R→E→X→C. P1 = 1 × G1 × G2 = 6/((s+1)(s+2)).
No other loops and no loop pairs, so Δ = 1 − L1 = 1 + 6/((s+1)(s+2)) = (s² + 3s + 8)/((s+1)(s+2)).
The loop uses nodes E, X, C, so it touches P1 and Δ1 = 1.
Check at s = 1: G1 = 2/2 = 1, G2 = 3/3 = 1, so P1 = 1, L1 = −1, Δ = 2, T = 0.5. Direct formula gives 6/(1 + 3 + 8) = 6/12 = 0.5. Poles are at s = (−3 ± j√23)/2, both in the left half plane.
examples.answer: C(s)/R(s) = 6/(s² + 3s + 8); at s = 1 the gain is 0.5, matching P1 = 1 with Δ = 2.
examples.check:
s = 1.0
g1 = 2/(s+1)
g2 = 3/(s+2)
H = 1.0
P1 = g1*g2
L1 = -g1*g2*H
delta = 1 - L1
T = P1/delta
print(P1)
print(delta)
print(T)

traps: Calling two loops non-touching when they share one node. One common node means touching, so no LiLj term exists for that pair.
Writing Δk = 1 blindly. Δk = 1 only when the path touches every loop; a non-touching loop must stay in Δk.
Dropping the minus sign of the feedback branch. Then Δ = 1 − |L1| instead of 1 + |L1|, and the denominator loses its correct sign.
Counting the same loop twice, once clockwise and once anticlockwise. A loop is defined by its set of nodes.
Using Δ1 for every forward path in a graph with two or more forward paths.

quiz.q: Define forward path gain Pk, loop gain Li and non-touching loops.
quiz.a: Pk is the product of branch gains on a source-to-sink path that visits no node twice. Li is the product of branch gains around a closed path that meets no node twice, with sign. Loops are non-touching when they share no node.

quiz.q: Write Mason's gain formula and name every symbol.
quiz.a: T = (ΣPkΔk)/Δ, where Pk is the k-th forward path gain, Δk is the cofactor of that path, and Δ = 1 − ΣLi + ΣLiLj − … is the graph determinant.

quiz.q: Why does Δk equal 1 when the forward path touches every loop?
quiz.a: Δk is Δ with all loops touching the path removed. If every loop touches the path, all loop terms are removed and only the leading 1 of Δ remains.

quiz.q: In the worked example, what does the branch C→E of gain −1 mean physically, and what happens to Δ if the minus sign is lost?
quiz.a: It means the feedback signal is subtracted from the input at the summing node. With the sign lost, Δ = 1 − 6/((s+1)(s+2)) = (s² + 3s − 4)/((s+1)(s+2)), which gives T = 6/(s² + 3s − 4) with a pole at s = +1, an unstable system.

quiz.q: A graph has one forward path P1 = 12 and two loops L1 = −2 and L2 = −4 that do not touch each other. Find T.
A graph has P1 = 4 and P2 = 2. Loop L1 = −1 touches both paths; loop L2 = −0.5 touches only P1. L1 and L2 touch each other. Find T.
quiz.a: Δ = 1 − (−1 − 0.5) = 2.5, with no non-touching pair. Δ1 = 1 (touches both loops). Δ2 = 1 − L2 = 1.5. T = (4×1 + 2×1.5)/2.5 = 7/2.5 = 2.8.

quiz.q: Why may a forward path not pass through the same node twice?
quiz.a: Passing a node twice would make the path contain a loop. Then the same signal would be counted both as a direct route and as a route through the loop, and Mason's formula would double-count it; loops are handled separately by Δ.

quiz.q: Two loops meet at one node out of six. A student keeps the pair in the ΣLiLj term. Describe the effect on Δ and on the pole locations.
quiz.a: An extra product term (positive, since both loop gains are negative) is added to Δ, so the denominator polynomial gains a wrong constant term. The poles shift and the time response of the predicted system no longer matches the hardware.

beyond: Not for the exam. Mason's rule is still the standard hand method in analog circuit design, where a feedback amplifier has nested loops and no clean block diagram. Symbolic circuit analysers build the same graph from the netlist and evaluate the determinant automatically. In control theory the graph view leads to the state-space model, where loops become feedback paths in the A matrix — see Unit 6, State Space Analysis. Search 'signal flow graph', 'Mason's rule' and 'graph determinant' for more.
